title: PCSX2 turns GSRunner dump playback into a repeatable renderer benchmark
summary: Unlimited playback and an opt-in performance report expose frame-time distribution, thread usage, GPU time, and rendering operation counts instead of measuring a dump through a 30 or 60 FPS cap.
heroAlt: Visual evidence from PCSX2 pull request #13751: GSRunner: Disable framerate limit in runner and dump frame timing stats.

sourceLabels.pcsx2-pr-13751: GSRunner: Disable framerate limit in runner and dump frame timing stats.

blocks.text: A frame limiter hides how fast a graphics dump can actually run

GSRunner replays captured GS command streams for renderer testing. When that playback remains capped to the original game's presentation rate, two implementations can both report 60 FPS even if one finishes the work much sooner. Pull request #13751 selects unlimited frame-limit mode in the runner, separating emulated presentation cadence from the throughput of the renderer being measured.
The -perf switch reports distribution and subsystem cost

An optional command-line switch prints minimum, average, and maximum frame times and their equivalent FPS. The same report includes CPU-thread, GS-thread, and GPU usage and average time, plus draw calls, render passes, barriers, copies, uploads, and readbacks. Those counters explain why a result changed: a slower average accompanied by more barriers is more actionable than a single throughput number.
Performance output stays opt-in and machine-readable enough to compare

Normal dump testing does not need the extra report, so the statistics are gated behind -perf. The emitted @HWSTAT@ lines give automation a stable marker without changing the dump itself. Minimum and maximum values prevent an average from hiding a single expensive frame, while separate CPU, GS, and GPU timing points indicate whether a regression moved work between threads rather than simply adding it.
A valid benchmark fixes the dump, renderer, and warm-up policy

Testing should first confirm that uncapped playback exceeds the source game's 30 or 60 FPS when the machine has headroom. Comparative runs must use the same dump, backend, resolution, shader cache state, power mode, and number of frames. Capture several repetitions, exclude a documented warm-up interval, and compare the full frame-time range and operation counters. Output correctness still requires the normal frame comparison; faster wrong frames are not a successful result.
GSRunner now measures renderer throughput rather than presentation rate, while its counters preserve enough context to explain where the time went.
